flashcards.q: What's the core mechanism of the dual-secret rotation pattern, and what happens if you skip the grace period?
flashcards.a: Maintain both old and new credentials as simultaneously valid across a grace period long enough for every reader to pick up the new one, then revoke the old one. Skipping the grace period (revoking old immediately) causes an outage for any reader still using the old credential.

flashcards.q: How do Vault dynamic secrets eliminate the rotation problem rather than just automate it?
flashcards.a: Each credential is generated per-lease, unique, TTL-bound, and auto-revoked at lease expiry by Vault -- there's no durable, long-lived secret sitting anywhere that ever needs rotating.

flashcards.q: What's the hard constraint that rules out legacy applications from using Vault dynamic secrets?
flashcards.a: The application must be lease-aware -- able to request or renew a fresh credential before the current lease expires. A legacy app reading a static connection string once at startup can't participate without a code refactor.

flashcards.q: Why does a JWT have no built-in revocation mechanism, and what's the consequence for TTL choice?
flashcards.a: JWTs are verified locally via signature check with no network call to a central authority -- there's no mechanism to invalidate a specific token before its exp claim. This makes TTL a direct bound on how long a compromised/revoked token stays dangerous, driving the 2026 consensus of 5-15 minute access tokens.

flashcards.q: What are the 2026 consensus TTL ranges for JWT access tokens and refresh tokens?
flashcards.a: Access tokens: 5-15 minutes. Refresh tokens: 7-30 days, and unlike access tokens, refresh tokens ARE actually revocable server-side since they're checked against a store on every use.

flashcards.q: Explain refresh token rotation with reuse detection.
flashcards.a: Every refresh token is single-use: using it mints a new access token AND a new refresh token, invalidating the one just used. A replay of an already-rotated (invalidated) refresh token is a theft signal, since two parties tried to use the same credential -- the correct response is revoking the entire token family, not just the flagged token.

flashcards.q: Why revoke the entire token family, not just the one reused refresh token, on reuse detection?
flashcards.a: By the time reuse is detected, the attacker may have already used the stolen token to mint further descendant refresh tokens -- revoking only the flagged token would leave those descendants still valid.

flashcards.q: What does adding a Redis-backed JWT deny list cost, and how do you avoid paying it on every request?
flashcards.a: An O(1) lookup (~50KB storage per 10,000 revoked entries) but still a network round-trip per check. Cache the 'not revoked' result locally with a short TTL (seconds), chosen against the actual revocation-propagation SLA needed -- otherwise the cache itself reintroduces the staleness the deny list was meant to eliminate.

flashcards.q: What actually happens when an admin revokes a user's session in a pure short-TTL-JWT, no-deny-list design?
flashcards.a: The refresh token is invalidated immediately (no new access tokens can be minted), but any already-issued access token remains valid until its own exp -- up to the full access-token TTL (5-15 min) of lag before revocation fully takes effect.

flashcards.q: What does a Secrets Manager rotation Lambda's finishSecret step do with the old credential, and why not delete it?
flashcards.a: Demotes it to AWSPREVIOUS rather than deleting it, providing an immediate rollback path if the newly-promoted AWSCURRENT credential turns out to have a problem shortly after rotation completes.

flashcards.q: How do you correctly determine the grace period length for a dual-secret rotation?
flashcards.a: It must exceed the slowest reader's actual refresh interval -- cache TTL, restart/deploy cadence, whichever is longest -- not a fixed arbitrary number. Too short causes an outage; needlessly long delays closing the exposure window if the rotation was leak-driven.

flashcards.q: Why isn't caching JWT signature-verification results the same class of optimization as caching a deny-list lookup?
flashcards.a: Signature verification is a local cryptographic operation with no network call, negligible cost to begin with. Deny-list lookup caching avoids a genuinely real network round-trip to Redis on every request -- a meaningful cost to optimize, unlike signature verification.
